```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 3.6, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
```

BATTS compares two samples by estimating the ratio `p/q` of their densities.
It implements the two additive tree methods of Awaya, Xu, and Ma (2025):
a boosting estimator, which gives a point estimate, and a generalized
Bayesian model with additive trees, which also gives posterior draws and
hence credible bands for the ratio.

Both methods estimate the balancing weight `w = sqrt(p/q)`. The `predict()`
and `fitted()` methods transform it, and by default return the log-density
ratio `log(p/q) = 2 * log(w)`. A positive value means that the first sample is
denser than the second at that point.

```{r library}
library(BATTS)
```

## Simulated two-sample data

This vignette considers four pairs of distributions, two in one dimension
and two in two dimensions. For each pair we keep the true log-density ratio
so that the estimates can be compared with it.

### Location shift in one dimension

The first sample comes from `N(0, 1)` and the second from `N(0.5, 1)`. The
true log-density ratio is a straight line.

```{r data-location}
set.seed(12345)
n1 <- 250L
loc <- list(x = rnorm(n1), y = rnorm(n1, mean = 0.5))
loc_truth <- function(t) dnorm(t, log = TRUE) - dnorm(t, mean = 0.5, log = TRUE)
```

### Scale difference in one dimension

Both samples are centred at zero, with standard deviations 1 and 1.5. The
true log-density ratio is a downward parabola: the first sample is denser in
the middle and the second in the tails.

```{r data-scale}
set.seed(23456)
scl <- list(x = rnorm(n1), y = rnorm(n1, sd = 1.5))
scl_truth <- function(t) dnorm(t, log = TRUE) - dnorm(t, sd = 1.5, log = TRUE)
```

### Global shift in two dimensions

This is Scenario 1 of Awaya, Xu, and Ma (2025): two correlated normal
distributions that differ by a shift of one unit in the first coordinate.
The true log-density ratio is linear.

```{r data-global}
log_dnorm2 <- function(x, mean, sigma) {
  z <- sweep(x, 2, mean) %*% solve(chol(sigma))
  -0.5 * rowSums(z^2) - log(2 * pi) - 0.5 * log(det(sigma))
}
rnorm2 <- function(n, mean, sigma) {
  sweep(matrix(rnorm(2 * n), n, 2) %*% chol(sigma), 2, mean, "+")
}

sigma_g <- matrix(c(2, 0.4, 0.4, 1), 2, 2)
set.seed(34567)
n2 <- 1000L
glb <- list(x = rnorm2(n2, c(0, 0), sigma_g), y = rnorm2(n2, c(1, 0), sigma_g))
glb_truth <- function(x) {
  log_dnorm2(x, c(0, 0), sigma_g) - log_dnorm2(x, c(1, 0), sigma_g)
}
```

### Local shift in two dimensions

This is Scenario 2 of the paper. Both samples are equal mixtures of three
normal components with standard deviation 0.3. In the second sample, only the
third component is shifted, by one standard deviation in the first
coordinate. The two densities therefore agree except near that component.

```{r data-local}
centres <- rbind(c(-2.5, 1), c(1, -2), c(2, 2.5))
rmix <- function(n, centres) {
  k <- sample.int(3L, n, replace = TRUE)
  centres[k, ] + matrix(rnorm(2 * n, sd = 0.3), n, 2)
}
dmix <- function(x, centres) {
  dens <- sapply(1:3, function(k) {
    dnorm(x[, 1], centres[k, 1], 0.3) * dnorm(x[, 2], centres[k, 2], 0.3)
  })
  rowMeans(dens)
}

shifted <- centres
shifted[3, ] <- centres[3, ] + c(-0.3, 0)
set.seed(45678)
lcl <- list(x = rmix(n2, centres), y = rmix(n2, shifted))
lcl_truth <- function(x) log(dmix(x, centres)) - log(dmix(x, shifted))
```

## Fit the models

The settings of each method are collected by `boost_control()` and
`bart_control()`. Their defaults are the settings used in the simulations of
the paper. Here we use boosting trees of depth 2, which give a smoother
estimate than the default depth 4 in these small examples, and a shorter
Markov chain (100 trees, 300 burn-in iterations and 301 saved draws) so that
the vignette builds quickly. These shorter chains are for illustration and
are not a recommendation for applied work.

```{r controls}
boost_ctl <- boost_control(depth = 2)
bart_ctl <- bart_control(num_trees = 100, burnin = 300, draws = 301,
                         keep_draws = TRUE)
```

The two samples can be passed directly as `x` and `y`; `x` is then the
numerator `p`. Setting `keep_draws = TRUE` saves the posterior forests, so
that the Bayesian fit can later be evaluated at new points.

```{r fit-1d}
set.seed(56789)
loc_boost <- batts_boost(loc$x, y = loc$y, control = boost_ctl, quiet = TRUE)
loc_bart <- batts_bart(loc$x, y = loc$y, control = bart_ctl, quiet = TRUE)
scl_boost <- batts_boost(scl$x, y = scl$y, control = boost_ctl, quiet = TRUE)
scl_bart <- batts_bart(scl$x, y = scl$y, control = bart_ctl, quiet = TRUE)
```

## Inspect fitted objects

Printing a fit summarizes the data, the ensemble and the direction of the
ratio.

```{r print}
loc_boost
loc_bart
```

`summary()` adds the fitted domain, outside of which the fit cannot be
evaluated, and the range of the fitted weights.

```{r summary}
summary(loc_boost)
```

`plot()` gives a quick diagnostic. For a boosting fit it shows the
cross-validation loss against the number of trees, with the selected number
marked. For a Bayesian fit it shows the trace of the loss temperature across
the saved draws.

```{r diagnostics}
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
plot(loc_boost)
plot(loc_bart)
par(old_par)
```

## Evaluate the fitted density ratios

We evaluate both fits on a grid covering the central 95% of the pooled data.
For the Bayesian fit, `interval = TRUE` returns the posterior mean together
with a pointwise credible band.

```{r evaluate-1d}
ratio_curves <- function(sample, boost, bart, truth) {
  grid <- seq(quantile(c(sample$x, sample$y), 0.025),
              quantile(c(sample$x, sample$y), 0.975), length.out = 200)
  list(grid = grid, truth = truth(grid), boost = predict(boost, grid),
       band = predict(bart, grid, interval = TRUE, level = 0.95))
}
loc_curves <- ratio_curves(loc, loc_boost, loc_bart, loc_truth)
scl_curves <- ratio_curves(scl, scl_boost, scl_bart, scl_truth)
head(loc_curves$band, 3)
```

The helper below draws the band in grey, the posterior mean as a solid line,
the boosting estimate as a dotted line and the truth as a dashed line.

```{r evaluate-1d-plot}
draw_ratio <- function(curves, main) {
  band <- curves$band
  plot(curves$grid, band[, "fit"], type = "n",
       ylim = range(band, curves$truth, curves$boost),
       xlab = "x", ylab = "log(p/q)", main = main)
  polygon(c(curves$grid, rev(curves$grid)),
          c(band[, "lower"], rev(band[, "upper"])), col = "grey85", border = NA)
  abline(h = 0, col = "grey60")
  lines(curves$grid, curves$truth, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
  lines(curves$grid, curves$boost, col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2, lty = 3)
  lines(curves$grid, band[, "fit"], lwd = 2)
}

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
draw_ratio(loc_curves, "Location shift")
legend("topright", c("truth", "boosting", "posterior mean", "95% band"),
       col = c("red", "darkgreen", "black", "grey85"), lty = c(2, 3, 1, 1),
       lwd = c(2, 2, 2, 8), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
draw_ratio(scl_curves, "Scale difference")
par(old_par)
```

Both fits follow the line and the parabola over most of the range. The
credible band is narrow where the data are dense and widens towards the tails,
where few observations inform the ratio and the estimates are drawn towards
zero.

Other scales are available through `type`: `density_ratio()` returns `p/q`
itself, and `type = "weight"` returns the balancing weight `w = sqrt(p/q)`.

```{r scales}
density_ratio(loc_boost, c(-1, 0, 1))
predict(loc_bart, c(-1, 0, 1), type = "weight")
```

## Two-dimensional examples

The two-dimensional samples are matrices with one column per variable, and
are fitted in the same way. Since we only evaluate these fits at the observed
points, we do not keep the posterior forests.

```{r fit-2d}
bart_ctl_2d <- bart_control(num_trees = 100, burnin = 300, draws = 301)
set.seed(67890)
glb_boost <- batts_boost(glb$x, y = glb$y, control = boost_ctl, quiet = TRUE)
glb_bart <- batts_bart(glb$x, y = glb$y, control = bart_ctl_2d, quiet = TRUE)
lcl_boost <- batts_boost(lcl$x, y = lcl$y, control = boost_ctl, quiet = TRUE)
lcl_bart <- batts_bart(lcl$x, y = lcl$y, control = bart_ctl_2d, quiet = TRUE)
```

As in the paper, we colour the observations by the value of the log-density
ratio, using a common scale for the truth and both estimates. Red points mark
where the first sample is denser and blue points where the second is. The last
panel shows the posterior standard deviation, the two-dimensional counterpart
of the width of the credible band.

```{r draw-2d}
diverging <- hcl.colors(101, "Blue-Red 3")
sequential <- hcl.colors(101, "YlOrRd", rev = TRUE)
draw_points <- function(x, value, limits, palette, main) {
  index <- round((pmin(pmax(value, limits[1]), limits[2]) - limits[1]) /
                   diff(limits) * 100) + 1
  ord <- order(abs(value - mean(limits)))
  plot(x[ord, ], col = palette[index[ord]], pch = 16, cex = 0.5, asp = 1,
       xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2", main = main)
}
draw_scenario <- function(sample, boost, bart, truth) {
  x <- rbind(sample$x, sample$y)
  true_value <- truth(x)
  limits <- c(-1, 1) * max(abs(true_value))
  draws <- fitted(bart, summary = "none")
  old_par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
  on.exit(par(old_par))
  draw_points(x, true_value, limits, diverging, "true log(p/q)")
  draw_points(x, fitted(boost), limits, diverging, "boosting")
  draw_points(x, rowMeans(draws), limits, diverging, "posterior mean")
  sds <- apply(draws, 1, sd)
  draw_points(x, sds, c(0, max(sds)), sequential, "posterior SD")
}
```

For the global shift, both estimates reproduce the linear trend along the
first coordinate.

```{r plot-global, fig.height = 6.4}
draw_scenario(glb, glb_boost, glb_bart, glb_truth)
```

For the local shift, the truth is zero on the first two components and
changes sign across the third, where the second sample has moved to the left.
Both estimates locate this blue and red pair, and show only faint colour on the
unchanged components. The posterior standard deviation is largest around the
shifted component.

```{r plot-local, fig.height = 6.4}
draw_scenario(lcl, lcl_boost, lcl_bart, lcl_truth)
```

## Practical notes

- `x` and `y` may be numeric matrices, data frames with numeric columns, or,
  for one variable, numeric vectors. Instead of `y`, a single sample can be
  given with a `group` vector of two labels; the first level (or the smaller
  value) is the numerator `p`. `print()` always states the direction.
- A fit can only be evaluated inside its fitted domain, the range of the
  training data widened by `margin_scale` (10% by default). `predict()` stops
  for other points unless `outside = "na"` or `outside = "clamp"` is given.
  Columns of `newdata` are matched by name when both sides have names.
- Evaluating a Bayesian fit at new points requires
  `bart_control(keep_draws = TRUE)`. With the default 200 trees and 1000
  draws the saved forests can exceed 100 MB, so keep them only when needed.
  `fitted()` and `predict()` without `newdata` work in either case.
- Set the seed before fitting. Cross-validation folds, subsamples and the
  Markov chain use the R random number generator; prediction does not.
- The short chains used above illustrate the interface. For substantive
  analyses, use longer chains, run several of them and check their agreement.
  The bands are pointwise; that a band contains zero does not show that the
  two distributions are equal.
- `boots()`, `batts()` and `eval_balance_weight()`, the interface of
  versions before 0.4.0, still work and give the same results, but are
  deprecated. See `` ?`BATTS-deprecated` `` for the correspondence of the
  arguments.

## References

Awaya, N., Xu, Y., and Ma, L. (2025). Two-sample comparison through additive
tree models for density ratios. arXiv:2508.03059.
<https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2508.03059>
